Featured.title: Some of what we've built
Featured.description: Each table is a negotiation between one board and the resin poured into it. These are the pieces that show best how we settle it.

MadeForSpace.title: Built for one room.
MadeForSpace.description: Your room fixes the dimensions. Your slab fixes the character. Neither one gets picked out of a catalogue.

items.title: You choose the actual slab
items.description: Once your deposit clears we go looking for three to five boards that suit your measurements. Each is photographed dry, then wetted so the grain reads the way it finally will. You choose from those. Nothing meets a saw before you do.

items.title: Built to your dimensions
items.description: Describe the room to us, not the table. We will tell you what genuinely fits, what turns cramped the moment chairs are pulled out, and what is never getting through your doorway.

items.title: Finished by hand
items.description: Machines get the top flat. Hands take it the rest of the way. Wood and resin abrade at different rates, so the seam between them is judged with fingertips rather than eyes.

Testimonials.title: What our clients say.
Testimonials.subtitle: Every table is made for one room and one client. What they say about it belongs with the piece.
Testimonials.body: Every Benzart Resin table is made to order, one at a time, and we are still collecting written accounts from the people living with them. We would rather leave this space empty than fill it with words we wrote ourselves.
Testimonials.secondary: Until then, the work puts it more precisely than a pull-quote could. Every piece in the collection is documented with the slab it came from, the resin poured into it, and the decisions that shaped it.

walnut-berber-resin-coffee-table.name: Walnut Coffee Table with Berber Motif Resin River
walnut-berber-resin-coffee-table.resinColor: Opaque black with embroidered Berber panel
walnut-berber-resin-coffee-table.story: A live-edge coffee table in solid walnut, split down its length by a channel of black epoxy that holds a hand-embroidered Berber panel. Cross-stitch diamonds, chevrons and X-forms in white, gold, green, rust and violet sit suspended under a mirror-gloss pour, so the pattern reads clearly from standing height. Both walnut slabs keep their natural edge and the pale sapwood line that runs with it. The base is cut from the same timber: two solid planks, live-edged, carrying the top without an apron. Finished at 120 x 75 cm.

oval-walnut-navy-resin-dining-table.name: Oval Walnut Dining Table with Navy Resin River
oval-walnut-navy-resin-dining-table.resinColor: Deep navy with pearl and grey marbling
oval-walnut-navy-resin-dining-table.story: An oval dining table in solid walnut, its ends fully radiused so nothing catches as chairs are pulled out. Two book-matched walnut slabs are held apart by a river of deep navy epoxy, marbled with pearl and grey where the pour caught the light. It reads almost black indoors and resolves to true navy in daylight. The inner edges are the tree's own, left exactly as the slab gave them. The walnut carries heavy figure and burl through both halves, and the whole top is finished to a mirror gloss on splayed walnut legs. Seats six at 180 x 90 cm.

walnut-3d-textured-clear-resin-dining-ta.name: Walnut Dining Table with 3D-Textured Clear Resin
walnut-3d-textured-clear-resin-dining-ta.resinColor: Clear to smoky sage green, 3D cellular relief
walnut-3d-textured-clear-resin-dining-ta.story: A rectangular dining table built the other way round: one broad slab of solid walnut runs down the centre, and the epoxy sits to either side of it rather than between two boards, forming the finished outer edges. The resin is poured almost clear, tinted a pale smoky sage, and carries a deep three-dimensional cell relief — domed cells standing proud of the surface that throw light differently as you move around the table. The walnut is the reason for the piece, a single board of heavy red-brown burl figure with its live edge kept on both flanks. Polished to a mirror and set on a black steel trapezoid frame. Seats six to eight at 180 x 90 cm.

walnut-smoke-resin-dining-table.name: Walnut Dining Table with Smoke Resin River
walnut-smoke-resin-dining-table.story: A rectangular dining table in solid walnut, lighter and more golden than most of the boards that come through the workshop, with the pale sapwood line left intact along both river edges. Between the two slabs runs a river of translucent charcoal epoxy that reads as smoke in the shallows and near black where it is deepest — clear enough that the floor and whatever stands on the table show through it — so the walnut either side keeps all the attention. The top is polished to a mirror and carried on a black steel closed-loop sled frame that keeps the legs clear of knees. Seats six at 175 x 85 cm.

walnut-turquoise-resin-dining-table.name: Walnut Dining Table with Turquoise Epoxy River
walnut-turquoise-resin-dining-table.story: A rectangular dining table in solid walnut, opened down the middle by a deep pour of translucent turquoise epoxy that deepens to emerald where it is thickest. The river keeps the rounded cell structure the resin took as it set, standing proud of the surface, so it reads as moving water rather than flat colour. The bark lines and voids along both live edges are filled opaque black — a deliberate contrast that holds the outline rather than hiding a fault. Both outer edges follow the tree, their notches filled flush so the perimeter finishes straight. The walnut is dense and strongly figured, sanded and polished to a mirror before it was set on a black steel trapezoid frame. Seats six to eight at 180 x 90 cm.

walnut-emerald-resin-geometric-lattice-t.name: Walnut Table with Green Resin over a Geometric Lattice
walnut-emerald-resin-geometric-lattice-t.resinColor: Bottle green to sage over a 3D geometric lattice
walnut-emerald-resin-geometric-lattice-t.story: The most technical piece in the collection. Set beneath the resin is a tessellated geometric lattice — a field of interlocking triangles resolving into six-pointed stars — and it is not printed or flat: each facet is raised in pyramidal relief, so the pattern has real depth while the surface above it stays perfectly flat glass. The green shifts with thickness and light, from bottle green where the pour encapsulates the outer live edges, through emerald with cream marbling in the margins, to a pale sage over the lattice itself. The walnut runs warm and golden with dark mineral streaks and natural voids, its live edge kept on both sides and frozen inside the resin so the perimeter finishes straight. Mirror polished and mounted on a black steel U-frame. 150 x 75 cm, seating four.

round-walnut-emerald-resin-coffee-table.name: Round Walnut Coffee Table with Emerald Resin River
round-walnut-emerald-resin-coffee-table.story: A round coffee table cut from solid walnut, one metre across, with a river of green epoxy crossing it off-centre so the circle never reads as symmetrical. The colour is not one green: it runs emerald through the body of the river, lifts to a bright turquoise where the pour is thin and light passes through it, and sinks to near-black bottle green in the deeper pools. The walnut carries dense flame and cathedral figure with a pale honey sapwood zone against the resin, and its small natural voids were stabilised and filled before the top was polished to a mirror. Raised on a black steel base so the whole disc appears to float. 100 cm diameter, at coffee-table height.

solid-walnut-live-edge-dining-table-220.name: Solid Walnut Live-Edge Dining Table, 220 cm
solid-walnut-live-edge-dining-table-220.story: No resin river on this one, and it does not need one. This is a single long board of solid walnut, 220 cm, left to do all the work itself: heavy rippled figure through the centre, dark mineral streaking, and the natural edge kept on both sides exactly as the tree grew it, so the outline is a rectangle only in the general sense. The checks and voids were stabilised and filled to make the surface sound, and those fills read as dark glassy pools rather than disappearing — they are part of how the piece looks, not hidden repairs. The top was finished to a low sheen rather than a gloss, which is the honest choice for a board with this much movement in the grain. Set on a black steel base with the legs inset, so both ends are usable. Seats eight at 220 x 85 cm.

walnut-woven-carpet-resin-dining-table.name: Walnut Dining Table with Woven Carpet Under Resin
walnut-woven-carpet-resin-dining-table.resinColor: Milky sage-white over a woven carpet panel
walnut-woven-carpet-resin-dining-table.story: A rectangular dining table where a hand-woven carpet panel is sealed under milky epoxy and set against a slab of pale walnut. The weave keeps its ridges and its banded stripes — ivory and cream alternating with taupe and soft brown, some bands carrying small diamond motifs — visible through the resin but protected from everything a dining table has to survive. The resin is only semi-translucent, with a faint sage-grey cast, so it veils the textile softly rather than showing it under glass. This is an unusually pale, blonde board with dark purple-black streaking rather than the dark heartwood of the other pieces, and its live edge follows the tree along the whole length. Finished satin, not gloss, and carried on a hand-built wooden trestle frame. Seats six at 180 x 90 cm.

resin-oval-dining-table.name: Oval Marble-Effect Resin Dining Table
resin-oval-dining-table.resinColor: Chocolate brown and ivory marble effect
resin-oval-dining-table.story: An oval dining table finished as a single sweep of marble-effect resin. Deep chocolate brown, shot through with oxblood and warm tan, is pulled apart by an ivory vein that meanders the length of the table and breaks out into broad cream fields at one side and around the ends. Fine white veining and discrete white spatter sit inside the dark ground, where the pigments were allowed to break rather than blend. Every one is different because the pour cannot be repeated. The marbling continues over the rim onto the vertical edge, so the top reads as one solid material rather than a surface laid on something else. Straight sides with fully radiused ends, polished to a high gloss and carried on a black steel base. Seats six at 160 x 80 cm.

walnut-resin-coffee-table-set.name: Walnut Coffee Table and Side Table Set with Magenta Resin
walnut-resin-coffee-table-set.story: Two pieces cut from the same walnut and finished together. The larger table takes a freeform kidney shape, its outline following the board rather than a drawing, with a wide S-curve river of translucent pink-red epoxy running the full length. The same colour was poured out to the finished perimeter, so it appears at the rim as well as mid-slab — though it breaks wherever the live edge reaches the outline, which is what gives the profile its rhythm rather than a continuous ring. The colour itself moves with the light: fuchsia under flat overhead daylight, crimson and raspberry in warm sun. The round side table repeats the idea at 50 cm across, a single band laid over dense burl figure, and stands slightly taller than the coffee table as a companion rather than a nesting piece. Both tops are mirror polished on black steel. Coffee table 120 x 75 cm, side table 50 cm diameter.

solid-walnut-live-edge-dining-table-180.name: Solid Walnut Live-Edge Dining Table, 180 cm
solid-walnut-live-edge-dining-table-180.story: A dining table for six with nothing added to it. One slab of solid walnut, chocolate brown through the centre with a broad band of pale sapwood following one edge, both long sides left live exactly as the board came off the mill — including a waisted notch on one side that no one straightened out. The figure is dense and strongly rippled, with a crotch eye near the middle and a hairline check running through it, filled flush. There is no resin river here and none was needed. The surface is finished satin rather than gloss, so it can be wiped down and used, and it never mirrors the room back at you. Carried on splayed walnut legs with a wooden cross member. 180 x 80 cm.

OurCraft.title: Our Craft.
OurCraft.description: One workshop on Ourika Road outside Marrakech, building a single table at a time for one specific room and one client.
OurCraft.philosophyHeading: We work between traditional joinery and material science.
OurCraft.philosophyBody1: Wood carries something no machine can fake: the record of one growing season, compressed into grain. Resin carries what wood cannot — depth you can look into, and a finish that can be renewed instead of replaced.
OurCraft.philosophyBody2: A table is the conversation between those two materials. Our job is making sure it is a conversation worth having.
OurCraft.studioBody1: Everything happens in one workshop in Marrakech. Boards are picked by hand. Every pour is mixed by weight rather than by eye, and every surface climbs through progressive grits before the hard-wax oil goes on.
OurCraft.studioBody2: We do not subcontract the joinery and we do not subcontract the finishing. If it carries our mark, it left our bench.
OurCraft.leadImageAlt: Finished walnut table with a vivid blue epoxy river, resting on trestles in the workshop
OurCraft.workshopAlt: Green epoxy resin being poured from a bucket into the mould around a walnut slab

phases.title: Consultation
phases.body: We talk through the room, the table, the materials and the budget. By the time the call ends you should know whether we are the right workshop for the piece — including if the answer is no.
phases.alt: Finished walnut dining table with a black resin river and six cream chairs in a client dining room

phases.title: Design
phases.body: You get one measured drawing and a material board. No three-dimensional render, because the slab is the design and no render can tell you what the grain will do. You approve it before anything is cut.
phases.alt: Completed walnut table with a black resin river and a sculpted timber base, in the workshop

phases.title: Selection
phases.body: Once your deposit clears we source three to five boards matching your dimensions and photograph each one dry, then wetted. You choose from those photographs. Nothing meets a saw until you have.
phases.alt: Craftsman guiding a rough walnut slab with its bark edge intact through a workshop bandsaw

phases.title: Production
phases.body: Eight to twelve weeks, depending on the season and how complex the pour is. Progress photographs come at three points: the pour, the flatten, and the first sanding coat.
phases.alt: Craftsman trimming the edge of a cured walnut and resin table top with a circular saw

phases.title: Delivery
phases.body: In Marrakech we deliver and install ourselves. For everywhere else we crate the table in-house and hand it to a freight forwarder who specialises in fine art and furniture.
phases.alt: Two Benzart Resin staff carrying a wrapped table through the doorway of a client villa

processFaq.question: How long does a commission take?
processFaq.answer: Eight to twelve weeks from cleared deposit to delivery in Marrakech. Most of that window is cure time between resin layers, and rushing it traps heat in the pour. International freight adds transit on top, which we confirm when you book.

processFaq.question: Can I see the slab before it is cut?
processFaq.answer: You have to. Every candidate board is photographed dry and again wetted, which is the only honest preview of how the finished grain will read. You choose from those photographs, and nothing meets a saw until you have.

processFaq.question: What are your payment terms?
processFaq.answer: A deposit locks both the commission and the slab. The balance falls due before the table leaves the workshop. We do not finance pieces and we do not run staged payments after the deposit.

processFaq.question: My delivery date is fixed. Can you work to it?
processFaq.answer: Sometimes. Tell us the date in your first message rather than after we have quoted, and we will say plainly whether it is achievable. We would rather lose the commission than agree to a date we know we will miss.

processFaq.question: Do you ship internationally?
processFaq.answer: Regularly. The crate is built in-house from ISPM 15 compliant timber and handed to a forwarder who moves fine art and furniture rather than general cargo. Tracking and a packing report come with every shipment.

processFaq.question: What if it arrives damaged?
processFaq.answer: Every commissioned piece is insured from the moment it leaves the bench until somebody signs for it. One practical tip: photograph the crate before you open it. That single photo settles a freight claim faster than anything else.

privacySections.body: When you enquire, we collect your name, email address, phone number if you provide it, and the details of your project. We do not collect payment information through this website.

privacySections.heading: How we use it
privacySections.body: Your information is used only to respond to your enquiry and to prepare a quote. We do not share it with third parties, and we do not use it for marketing unless you explicitly agree.

privacySections.heading: How long we keep it
privacySections.body: We keep enquiry records for seven years to satisfy accounting and warranty obligations. After that, the record is deleted unless you ask us to keep it.

privacySections.heading: Your rights
privacySections.body: You can ask us to correct, update, or delete your information at any time by emailing the studio directly. We will respond within ten working days.

termsSections.heading: Commission
termsSections.body: A commission begins when we confirm a design and receive a deposit. The deposit is non-refundable once materials have been sourced or the pour has been scheduled.

termsSections.heading: Design ownership
termsSections.body: The final table design belongs to you. We retain the right to document the making — photographs, video, and written process notes — unless you ask us not to.

termsSections.heading: Delivery and risk
termsSections.body: Risk passes to you when the table is signed for at the delivery address. International deliveries require a signature from an adult present at the address.

termsSections.heading: Limitation of liability
termsSections.body: Our liability is limited to the replacement or repair of the table itself. We are not liable for consequential loss, including damage to surrounding property or loss of use.

Faq.title: FAQ.
Faq.description: Cost, wood, aftercare, and the work we turn down. The commissioning steps are answered on the enquiry page; this covers everything else. If your question is missing, ask us directly.

items.question: How much does a custom resin table cost?
items.answer: Most dining commissions land between 3,000 and 15,000 USD. The slab is the biggest single variable: one wide, long, well-figured board can account for over a third of the total on its own. Dimensions, resin volume, the base and the destination make up the rest. Every quote is fixed in writing before work starts.

items.question: Which wood should I choose?
items.answer: Walnut for dark, dramatic grain that suits a river pour. Olive for tight, swirling figure in shorter pieces, since long clear olive boards barely exist. Maple when you want the resin to be the loud element rather than the timber. If you are undecided, tell us the room and we will shortlist two or three.

items.question: How do I look after it?
items.answer: Wipe spills reasonably promptly and keep it out of permanent direct sun. The finish is a hard-wax oil, so a worn patch can be spot-repaired in place rather than requiring the whole top to be stripped. Refresh it every couple of years and it will outlast you.

items.question: Will the resin yellow or crack?
items.answer: Cheap resin yellows. We pour in thin layers with a UV-stabilised system, which is slower and the main reason lead times run to twelve weeks. Cracking comes from heat, not age: a pan straight off the hob will leave a permanent depression, because epoxy softens well below the temperature of a hot dish. Use a trivet and the surface is genuinely durable.

items.question: Can you copy a table I have seen?
items.answer: Not exactly, and we will not pretend otherwise. Boards from the same tree differ in density and figure, so the grain pattern belongs to the original piece. We can build another table in the same design language, at the same standard, and it will be recognisably a sibling rather than a duplicate.

items.question: What do you not make?
items.answer: No outdoor tables, since UV and thermal movement will eventually win. No flat-pack, no mass production, nothing held in stock. We also turn down commissions where the budget and the dimensions genuinely do not meet, rather than quietly cutting corners to reach the number.
